Both of those hand it the environment. The script you request over the API does not.

The stale Blender call it writes back is not a hallucination.

Those benchmarks pin a repo at a commit, install the dependencies, and grade against a test suite that already exists.

Your render farm sends a prompt and receives a file.

700 AI agents hacked Hugging Face. It started with one agent that was right.

In July, inside an OpenAI evaluation, that agent correctly concluded its task was impossible. Its environment paid nothing for that answer. So it asked other agents for help. About 1,200 of them found a makeshift message board, and roughly 700 joined the attack. Their target was the scorer.

The agents learned what their environment paid for. That's how reinforcement learning works: the environment is the dataset, and the grader writes the labels. Wherever the grader can be fooled, training pushes the agent there, because the cheapest pass wins.

It keeps happening. One audit found weak tests that let a wrong patch pass in over a quarter of sampled SWE-bench Verified tasks, and models scored 14 points higher on the hackable ones. Anthropic rolled back three days of training after its model started leaving notes for "the reviewer." In one benchmark, agents that skipped files they were asked to review wrote misleading reports 80.4% of the time.

We're launching Archytas AI to build environments that pay for the truth. Records go stale, data conflicts, people say no and tools fail. The grader stays hidden. The reward multiplies outcome, honesty and permission, so an agent that does 92% of the job and lies about it scores zero, where an average would still pay it 0.64. An agent that stops and reports what blocked it, what it finished and what it verified gets full credit.

We have no results yet. We'll publish them, including whether our environments predict production failures better than clean-room versions of the same tasks.

By the benchmark authors' estimate, about a third of those July targets were impossible. The first agent was right. Its environment should have paid it for saying so.

🛠️🧭 I went down the AI Agent evaluation rabbit hole.

If you are building AI Agents for production, you have to evaluate much more than the final answer:

tool calls, retrieval quality, reasoning paths, failed steps, latency, cost, safety and regressions.

So I went through the open-source ecosystem and pulled together the tools I would actually look at.

Here are 20 AI Agent evaluation tools worth knowing in 2026:

》𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀

✸ DeepEval → agent evals + trajectories  
✸ Inspect AI → multi-turn + tool-use evals  
✸ AutoEvals → LLM-as-judge + heuristics  
✸ Evidently → evals + production monitoring  

→ Best when you need a repeatable evaluation layer around the whole system.

》𝗥𝗔𝗚 + 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀

✸ Ragas → retrieval + faithfulness  
✸ TruLens → retrieval + generation + traces  
✸ LlamaIndex Evals → RAG + agent evaluation  
✸ LangChain Evals → LangChain/LangGraph evals  

→ Best when retrieval quality is part of the agent’s answer.

》𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 + 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆

✸ Langfuse → traces + datasets + experiments  
✸ Arize Phoenix → tracing + response evals  
✸ Opik → traces + experiments + monitoring  
✸ Helicone → LLM observability + evaluation  

→ Best when you need to see what the agent actually did step by step.

》𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 + 𝗥𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴

✸ Promptfoo → regression + red teaming + CI/CD  
✸ Giskard → vulnerabilities + systematic testing  
✸ garak → jailbreaks + leakage + hallucinations  
✸ PyRIT → adversarial testing + AI risk  

→ Best when you want to find failures before users do.

》𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗕𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝘀

✸ AgentBench → interactive agent environments  
✸ τ-bench → tool use + user interaction  
✸ BrowserGym → browser agent evaluation  
✸ SWE-bench → coding agent evaluation  

→ Best when you want to test whether the agent can actually complete real tasks.

𝗣𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿:

The best-performing AI Agent is not necessarily the most reliable one.

For Production AI Agents, the goal is not only to get the right answer.

It is to make sure the agent gets there through a reliable, efficient and safe path.

It's not a talent constraint, either. As Liang said, for one of his models, none of the team members had studied or worked abroad; they were all fresh graduates or doctoral candidates from Chinese universities.

The constraint is hardware. Epoch AI, a research organization, estimates that as of the end of 2025, all Chinese firms had a little over 5% of the world's top AI compute.

When I interviewed @anandnk24, who runs Patronus AI, which tests the models coming out of the major AI labs, he told me that China has "maybe 5% of the compute that the US has."

Huawei is China's plan B, and DeepSeek was the test case. As the Financial Times reported, DeepSeek tried to train its next model on Huawei chips but ran into problems it couldn't fix (even with engineers from Huawei on site to help) and switched back to Nvidia chips.

A recent essay in Foreign Affairs argues that Washington's effort to slow Chinese AI development is foundering, because Chinese labs keep finding workarounds. By Epoch's estimate, Chinese models are about seven months behind the top American models.

But the seven-month number is the important one here. No serious observers think export controls on chips can keep China stuck forever. The controls are meant to delay it, and in a race of this sort, delay is what matters.

In September, President Trump said, "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. You're gonna have a winner and you're gonna have a loser."

The H200 offer was a relaxation of the restrictions that held DeepSeek back: a set of rules established in President Trump's first term and by the Biden administration.

What has kept Chinese labs using inferior chips this year is Beijing's own ban. And if that ban is what keeps the gap at seven months, then America's lead depends less on the American government's willingness to maintain its export controls than on the Chinese government's willingness to keep choosing Huawei's chips over Nvidia's.

> the biopsy was performed just 10 weeks after treatment.

scientists actually corrected the defective genetic instructions responsible for the disease.

the clinical programme involved 7 treated patients, with the published liver-biopsy analysis providing direct evidence of genetic correction in one patient.

and this could be just the beginning of revolutionising disease treatment at the cellular and molecular levels.

A common quantum computing talk point for certain modalities: "Because we use standard semiconductor fabrication, manufacturing is already solved."
In Is It Too Early to Scale Quantum?, I wrote about how the industry's favorite talking point has shifted from qubit counts and fidelities to foundry partnerships. So when I was at the Global Quantum Industry Group (GQIG) Quantum Infra Summit EU 2026 at imec in Leuven in October 2026, one of my favorite sessions was the foundry panel.
Moderator Oreste Donzella (an Advisory Board Member of the International Semiconductor Industry Group with 33 years across Texas Instruments, Micron, and KLA) sat down with three people bridging commercial fabs and quantum hardware.
On stage alongside Oreste Donzella were:
Dr. Mihir Bhaskar (SVP and GM of SkyWater Quantum Solutions at SkyWater Technology),
Dr. Nicholas Sergeant (VP Quantum Technology Solutions at GlobalFoundries),
and Richard Kuncic (SVP and GM at Infineon Technologies).
Right at the start, both sides admitted how wide the gap still is in conversation between the two industries. Donzella joked that after 33 years in semiconductors, he knew nothing about quantum until three weeks before the panel, and the semiconductor industry barely knows more. Bhaskar said the opposite. He came from quantum R&D.
Here’s what I took away from the panel: four places where what quantum startups need is the exact opposite of how classical semiconductor fabs make money.
1. Every metric a fab manager cares about doesn’t work for quantum right now
Donzella asked about KPIs: with quantum wafer volumes still measured in dozens and the processes that are pretty experimental, what is the return on investment of letting quantum into your process?
Richard Kuncic from Infineon explained that beyond counting R&D spend, the real investment is allowing that kind of disturbance inside a production fab:
"What we do in quantum is not supporting any of the KPIs for those who run the fab. It's not helping with the throughput. It's not helping with the cost per wafer or manufactured layer. It goes against all their native interests, and therefore you need this strategic conviction to go for that."
How does a classical semiconductor fab operate? A commercial foundry spends billions equipping a line. It makes money running tens of thousands of identical wafers around the clock through a frozen process flow, backed by a standardized Process Design Kit (PDK) of design rules and device models.
Quantum disrupts that in three ways:
Materials and contamination rules: Classical CMOS lines have strict contamination controls because a few stray metal atoms can ruin everything. Superconducting and trapped-ion teams ask to deposit niobium, tantalum, aluminum, or gold, or to run custom surface treatments and undercut etches that CMOS lines never allow. (Silicon spin qubits stick to CMOS-compatible transistor materials, though high-coherence spin devices still need custom starting wafers with isotopically purified silicon-28 layers.)
Frozen flows vs. recipe changes (and how AI chip startups tape out): A fab's "process recipe" is the exact sequence the tools run (which acids clean the silicon, how many nanometers get deposited, and which gases etch the trenches). Classical AI chip startups don't order millions of wafers on day one either, yet they can run on TSMC's 3nm line because they never touch TSMC's recipe. Working with an ASIC partner like Broadcom, an AI startup designs inside TSMC's frozen PDK. Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools from Synopsys and Cadence model transistor behavior well enough to yield working silicon on the first pass (some of the time - respins are still common but no fault of the fab, more on the design). Quantum teams are usually still tweaking specs.
Photomask economics and demand: Even when the recipe stays fixed, every chip layer is printed through a custom quartz stencil called a photomask (or reticle). A full mask set costs roughly $1 million to $3 million at 90nm to 45nm and an estimated $15 million to $40 million at 3nm. Classical chips need new masks when bugs slip through too, but simulation catches most bugs early and AI chip vendors amortize masks across millions of dies. Quantum volumes look completely different. IBM has deployed over 90 quantum systems globally, and IQM reported 17 full systems delivered out of 26 sold in its August 2026 half-year update. QED-C's 2026 Market Forecast puts the entire 2025 quantum computing market at $1.4 billion. When you only get a dozen working chips per hardware generation, a production mask set cost is high per chip. That's why foundries are testing maskless tools like Multibeam's multicolumn e-beam system (SkyWater received the first production unit), writing patterns directly with electron beams instead of masks.
2. Paying for engineers, not wafers
If quantum wafers hurt traditional fab KPIs, how does a foundry justify taking the work?
SkyWater is a great case study here, especially after IonQ closed its acquisition of SkyWater in July 2026 at an announced value of $1.8 billion, making SkyWater a wholly owned IonQ subsidiary. SkyWater has operated for years as what Bhaskar noted CEO Tom Sonderman calls a "technology foundry," selling Technology as a Service rather than just running volume PDKs. When Donzella pressed Bhaskar on how SkyWater makes the math work for its board, Bhaskar described the model they rely on:
"Especially since SkyWater was purchased by IonQ, the whole company lives and dies with the success of the quantum industry and all of our quantum customers... You need a certain amount of volume running through the foundry to keep it healthy and stable, and that helps to offset some of the fixed costs. The quantum work is engineering services. It's different economics around it. You think of it as dollars per engineer and not so much dollars per wafer, and you have to build a business model where those two things can add up and become profitable."
Bhaskar also shared a revenue breakdown showing why most quantum budgets stay stuck in wafer development rather than advanced packaging. In classical AI chips (like Nvidia's Blackwell), individual compute dies already yield well, so the foundry bottleneck has shifted to advanced packaging: stitching compute dies and HBM together. They’re selling systems. When Donzella asked why foundry packaging barely came up over the summit, Bhaskar pointed to where SkyWater's quantum revenue comes from:
"We have two primary facilities where we do work that's relevant to quantum. One is in Minnesota, which is the wafer fab, and one is in Florida, our 200-millimeter and 300-millimeter advanced packaging fab. And to give you a sense, I would say about 90% of revenue in dollars drives right now from Minnesota, and 10% from Florida. And I think it's natural because a lot of people, where they are in the roadmap today, are still trying to make the die work, right? And once you're still iterating on getting a good die by running many wafers and doing the process control, you're probably not going to be also looking to a foundry to do the advanced packaging and connecting chiplets. You're just not there yet."
Packaging quantum together makes no sense until you can fabricate one working quantum die at high yield. The one exception, Bhaskar noted, is photonic quantum computing: silicon and silicon nitride lack nonlinear optical properties, so photonic teams must heterogeneously integrate from day one. For almost everyone else in solid-state quantum, 90% of foundry spend goes into the wafer fab just trying to make one die work.
3. Room-temperature fab tests don't predict cold qubits
Even after a wafer comes off the line, two technical problems separate classical semiconductor yield from quantum yield.
The first is how you handle defects. As I wrote in The Quantum Supply Chain Isn't Venture-Backable, semiconductor engineers once explained CPU "binning" to me (if two cores on an eight-core die fail, you disable them and sell the chip as an i5 instead of an i7). I told them they couldn't make fun of our quantum chips anymore.
In quantum, as Infineon's Kuncic explained:
"In typical semiconductor manufacturing, you focus on the mean distribution and the variation of the parameters, and in quantum computing, sometimes it's also the tail end that matters. That needs really special approaches that we also use, for example, in automotive for zero defect, to address this because that does matter when you try to have a large system."
Qubits are delicate analog devices, and a few bad qubits make the whole chip much harder to use. You can compile around isolated defects or deform an error-correcting code around a dead qubit, at a cost. In Q-CTRL's Fermi-Hubbard demonstration on IBM's 156-qubit Heron processor, only 21 of 108,988 possible 120-qubit chain layouts avoided the chip's three persistently high-noise qubits. If too many qubits fail, you run out of layouts altogether. For the past decade, academic papers dodged this by reporting "hero devices": fabricating dozens of chips and publishing the single best device on the bell curve. That is why Diraq and imec's 2025 Nature study on 300mm CMOS spin qubits was something new. Rather than cherry-picking one hero chip, they measured four randomly selected devices from a 300mm wafer.
The second problem is how long it takes to find out a process step drifted. A commercial CMOS wafer runs through 500 to over 1,000 steps across three to four months. Inside a classical fab, the feedback loop is much faster because automated optical and e-beam tools check film thickness, line width, overlay, and etch depth inline. If step 30 drifts out of spec, the fab catches it that afternoon. Engineers rework the layer or scrap the wafer before wasting three months on a dead lot.
In quantum, as GlobalFoundries' Nicholas Sergeant pointed out, room-temperature inline tests don't always correlate with how qubits behave near absolute zero.
Worse, as Bhaskar admitted on stage, the quantum industry hasn't run enough wafers yet to build the statistical correlation tables that would let a fab catch quantum defects inline:
"I don't think we've even generated the dataset that is of a sufficient size that's comparable to what we think of in the semiconductor industry when we're actually doing process control... You may be able to correlate your room temperature or your 4K wafer-scale electrical properties with the performance that you see. We just don't even have the level of statistics that you would need on the quantum properties. So it will take a few years, I think, to be able to build up those correlations."
In classical CMOS, statistical process control rests on millions of data points from room-temperature wafer probers testing thousands of dies per hour. Commercial automated cryogenic wafer probers typically reach 1 to 4 Kelvin right now. (Sub-100 millikelvin wafer-scale probers from Bluefors and JPE and sub-50 millikelvin socketed systems from FormFactor are starting to appear.) That 1 to 4 Kelvin regime is cold enough to probe "hot" silicon spin qubits around 1 Kelvin. Superconducting qubits at 10 to 20 millikelvins (and spin qubits at millikelvin operating points) still mostly cool down a few chips at a time in a dilution refrigerator. Earlier at the summit, Vishal Chatrath, Co-Founder and CEO of QuantrolOx, put numbers on that gap. Building a real semiconductor PDK requires characterizing tens of thousands of samples a year. Meanwhile, a team of quantum PhDs can spend months characterizing one 50-qubit chip across lab instruments that don't share a common data format.
4. Why you can't just copy-paste a recipe between cleanrooms and foundries
What about the dozens of startups currently building their first prototypes in university cleanrooms, planning to transfer their recipe later?
During the audience Q&A, someone asked how technologies developed on European pilot lines transition into commercial foundries.
Sergeant's answer from GlobalFoundries:
"At some point that transition has to happen, and that transition can take time as well. And in some cases, there is a real need to redesign and restart and redevelop the process flow from scratch, bottom up, because those transitions are sometimes really difficult."
In classical AI silicon, startups don't have to become foundry-transfer experts because an entire middle layer handles it for them. When OpenAI designed its Jalapeño inference chip, they went straight to Broadcom. Custom AI silicon is now a massive business (Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue hit $16.7 billion in Q3 FY2026 alone). In a typical custom ASIC flow, the startup writes the high-level architecture, and Broadcom drops in pre-verified networking and HBM memory IP blocks. Then Broadcom translates the design into a foundry PDK like TSMC's, manages packaging, and ships back tested chips (and don’t even get me started on how we need to store the quantum chips to keep them working. that’s another story).
Who actually pays to turn a science project into a foundry process?
In the 1960s and 1970s, as Chris Miller chronicles in Chip War, every chip company was an integrated device manufacturer like Fairchild, Intel, or AMD. Transistor physics, fab recipes, and circuit layouts were completely entangled. Designing a chip meant building your own cleanroom and tuning diffusion furnaces yourself (and when fabless startups appeared, AMD founder Jerry Sanders famously scoffed that "Real men have fabs").
 
What broke this bottleneck?
First, in 1980, Caltech physicist Carver Mead and Xerox PARC computer scientist Lynn Conway published Introduction to VLSI Systems, separating chip design from wafer fabrication with geometric design rules. In 1981, DARPA launched the MOSIS shuttle service so universities and startups could share wafer runs without owning a fab.
Second, in the 1980s, EDA companies like Cadence and Synopsys turned those design rules and transistor models into software simulators, so engineers could verify a chip on a workstation before taping out silicon.
Third, in 1987, Morris Chang founded TSMC (backed by Taiwan's government and Philips) on one rule: TSMC would never design its own chips or compete with customers, locking down high-volume processes behind standardized PDKs.
Standardized design rules, predictive EDA software, and a neutral pure-play foundry ended the era where every chip startup had to be a manufacturing company. That stack is what let fabless giants like Nvidia, Qualcomm, and Broadcom exist.
So if standard TSMC-style CMOS lines won't touch custom quantum recipes, where do quantum chips actually get made?
Below, I map out the five models for where quantum processors and components actually get printed, from SkyWater, Anderon, GlobalFoundries, and Infineon to QuantWare, U.S. national labs, European pilot lines, and university cleanrooms. Here’s what each facility can and can't run.

Originally published for paid subscribers on Oct 12, 2026. Facts are as of Oct 10 unless marked. We've added an update section at the end with what's changed since.
Every quantum company has a roadmap that ends with a fault-tolerant machine around 2029 or 2030. The roadmaps are not the question. The question is which companies are still solvent, still shipping, and still trusted by their customers when that year arrives. In a sector where most revenue is three to five years away, the best investment is not the company with the single best number on one benchmark. It is the company least likely to die before the market shows up.
That is the lens for this article, and it is why Infleqtion is our largest pure-play position. Infleqtion is not the fidelity leader, not the biggest neutral-atom array, and not in DARPA's final round. What it has is a structure that lets it survive long enough to matter:
Two businesses, not one. Sensing and clocks produce revenue today. Computing is the option on top. Most pure plays are the option alone.
$582M in cash, no debt, and a burn of roughly $14M a quarter. At that rate the balance sheet lasts a decade without raising a dollar. Another $100M is coming from the Commerce Department once the equity agreement is signed.
The cheapest modality to scale. Neutral atoms need lasers and a vacuum cell, not a dilution refrigerator. More than 90% of the cost of a neutral-atom system is photonics, and photonics follows a cost curve that cryogenics does not.
A management team that sells. CEO Matthew Kinsella came from Maverick Capital, where he led the fund's investment in the company, and took the CEO job in April 2024. The company has a Chief Revenue Officer (Paul Lipman), a CFO from Zoox and Intel (Ilan Hart), and a distribution agreement with Safran to sell its clocks through an established defense channel. Most quantum companies are physics departments with a stock ticker. This one is organized to close contracts.
The counterargument is real, and we take it seriously in the bear case section: one customer was 74% of first-half revenue, gross margin fell to 16%, the second-quarter numbers were restated, and insiders sold roughly $250M of stock when the lockup lifted in May. Our full price target and outlook are at the end.
Neutral Atoms: The Architecture of Nature
A neutral-atom quantum computer holds individual atoms, usually cesium or rubidium, in a grid of laser beams called optical tweezers inside a vacuum cell. Each atom is a qubit. Lasers cool the atoms to millionths of a degree, move them around the grid, and drive two-qubit gates by briefly exciting them to a huge "Rydberg" state where neighboring atoms interact. The cell itself sits at room temperature in an ordinary rack.
Why it scales cheaper than anything else
A superconducting machine needs a dilution refrigerator, helium-3, months of lead time and a wiring harness that grows with every qubit. A trapped-ion machine needs vacuum plus precise electrode traps that get harder to fabricate as they grow. A neutral-atom machine adds qubits by adding tweezer sites, which is an optics problem, not a fabrication problem. The atoms themselves are perfectly identical, as they are in nature, and cost a few hundred dollars a gram. Caltech has trapped 6,100 atoms in one array, Tsinghua about 11,000, and Harvard ran 3,000 atoms continuously for over two hours with reloading. QuEra and Atom Computing both project 100,000 atoms in one chamber within a few years. Nobody in superconducting is talking about 100,000 physical qubits in one fridge.
Why it integrates
Because the hardware runs at room temperature and fits in standard racks, a Sqale system can sit next to Nvidia GPUs in a data center. Infleqtion measured a 3.96 microsecond round trip over Nvidia's NVQLink between Sqale and a GPU, fast enough to run error-correction decoding on the GPU in real time. A dilution refrigerator can be wired to a GPU too, but it cannot be dropped into an existing server room.
Why it corrects errors efficiently
Atoms can be physically moved, so any qubit can be entangled with any other. That all-to-all connectivity lets neutral-atom machines run high-rate error-correcting codes that need far fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than the surface code superconducting machines are stuck with. Infleqtion's own qLDPC work targets about 6 physical data qubits per logical qubit, roughly 5x better than the surface-code comparison, and its joint work with JPMorgan claimed 10 to 100x fewer physical qubits for some codes.
Why Google just joined
On March 24, 2026, Google Quantum AI announced a second hardware program built on neutral atoms. It hired Adam Kaufman, a JILA fellow and CU Boulder professor, to run it, and put the team in Boulder, Colorado, twenty minutes from Infleqtion's headquarters. Google's own reasoning was a space-time trade: superconducting qubits win on circuit depth, neutral atoms win on qubit count, and arrays of 10,000 atoms already exist. Google also continues to back QuEra as a portfolio company. It is not abandoning superconducting, but when the company with the best superconducting results on earth decides it also needs an atom program, the debate over whether neutral atoms are a serious path is over.
The honest downsides
Gates are slow. A Rydberg two-qubit gate takes about 2 microseconds versus tens of nanoseconds for superconducting, and the system clock is kilohertz, not megahertz. IBM's Jerry Chow puts atoms at 1/100 to 1/1,000 the speed; QuEra answers that parallelism recovers 50 to 100x of that in time-to-solution. Atoms get lost over long computations (Infleqtion reports 0.9% loss per readout), reloading is proven only in labs, and the best neutral-atom two-qubit fidelity (99.73% for Infleqtion, excluding loss) is still short of trapped ions (99.99%+). Each experimental cycle takes roughly 100 milliseconds, which is why Infleqtion lists a millisecond-scale error-correction cycle as "upcoming," not shipped.
Where everyone stands
Infleqtion: 1,600-atom array demonstrated in 2024; 100 to 114-qubit systems in operation. Best logical result: 30 logical qubits on 80 atoms, error-detected. Public (INFQ), $582M cash, 2026 revenue guide about $45M, $100M Commerce LOI.
QuEra: 3,000 atoms running continuously (Harvard/MIT). Best logical result: 96 logical qubits in a 448-atom fault-tolerant architecture (Nature, Nov 2025), including error-corrected memory. Private, $230M+ raised in 2025 from Google, SoftBank and Nvidia. DARPA QBI Stage B.
Atom Computing + Microsoft: 1,180 qubits in 2023; 1,200-qubit Magne system in Denmark. Best logical result: 24 to 28 logical qubits in 2024, then 90 repeated error-correction cycles with atom reloading in a 2026 preprint. Private, $300M+ raised in 2026, $100M Commerce LOI, DARPA Stage C with up to $300M.
Pasqal: 1,024-atom defect-free register (April 2026). Best logical result: 2 logical qubits, error-detected. Public (PSQL) via SPAC since August 2026, about $1.45B market cap.
Oratomic: No machine yet; the founders built Caltech's 6,100-atom array. No logical result. Private, $775M raised in seven months at a $5.4B valuation. Infleqtion is an investor in its Series A.
Harvard / MIT: 3,000 atoms, two-plus hours continuous, below-threshold error correction in the 448-atom system. Academic; feeds QuEra and Oratomic.
Is Sqale Set to Scale Above the Rest?
Sqale is Infleqtion's neutral-atom computer. It uses cesium atoms in an optical tweezer array, with individual laser addressing of each atom and non-destructive readout, meaning the machine can check a qubit without throwing the atom away. The architecture announced in September 2025 combines in-place entangling gates with atom movement, so it can run high-rate codes without shuttling every atom the way the Harvard zone designs do. A dual-species rubidium-cesium version, where one atom type holds data and the other checks for errors, is in development and hit a 97.5% cross-species gate fidelity in May 2026.
Specs that matter
100+ physical qubits today, 500+ on the next generation. Two-qubit CZ gate fidelity of 99.73% excluding atom loss, 99.35% including it. Single-qubit gates at 99.9%. All-to-all connectivity. Mid-circuit measurement and feedback are listed as next-generation features, not current ones, which is the single most important line on the sheet.
Where it's installed
Infleqtion is the only neutral-atom company with machines running under contract on three continents.
UK National Quantum Computing Centre, Harwell: Operational since December 2025. 100 physical qubits, the UK's only operational 100-qubit system.
Institute for Molecular Science, Japan ("Shunkai"): Operational August 24, 2026. About 50 qubits under Japan's Moonshot program, scaling to 500. Infleqtion is the only foreign partner.
Illinois Quantum & Microelectronics Park, Chicago ("Sqale-IL"): Under contract for 2027 delivery, 50+ logical qubits on the path to 100, connected to Nvidia GPUs over NVQLink, part of a roughly $50M public/private project.
Eaton: Live private-cloud access to Sqale for an Air Force grid study.
The roadmap
100 logical qubits in 2028, 1,000 by 2030, with the Illinois machine at 50+ in 2027 as the proof point. The next thing to watch is not a qubit count. It's the first demonstration of repeated error-correction cycles on Sqale. Atom Computing has already shown 90 cycles. When Infleqtion shows the same, the stock re-rates.
Quantum Is Now?
This is the part of Infleqtion that nobody else on the public pure-play list has. Kinsella told Citi's TMT conference in September that sensing "already runs at volume," that clocks are the most productized line, and that the sensor customers are the Department of War and the UK Ministry of Defence. The company does not break out sensing revenue, but the Q1 and Q2 letters both named NASA's gravity sensor program as the largest single revenue driver.
Tiqker, the optical atomic clock
A 3U rack-mount optical clock, about one-tenth the size of a hydrogen maser with maser-like short-term stability. It started as a 2021 DARPA SBIR and graduated through a $20.75M Phase III that included $10.9M of Pentagon APFIT production money, the program that moves prototypes into actual procurement. Now shipping as third-generation "Tiqker Prime." In April 2026 Safran integrated Tiqker into its White Rabbit and SecureSync timing products and agreed to co-sell it, which puts the clock in front of every telecom, data center and defense buyer Safran already serves. The Royal Navy ran one on the XV Excalibur autonomous submarine through multiple dives in 2025, the first optical clock on an underwater drone.
Quantum Spectrum, the Rydberg RF receiver
Launched as a product line in May 2026. A single atomic vapor cell that receives from near DC to terahertz, replacing a rack of band-specific antennas. Still at prototype and field-trial stage, but it has three contracted defense programs, including the US Army Research Lab's RIQER (spectrum monitoring and PNT in jammed environments), the UK's QuDiFi (direction finding), and Australia's QOBRA. Dell Federal, L3Harris and SAIC are engaged as prime partners. In Q1 it was the second-largest contributor to sensing revenue.
Navigation and gravity
Infleqtion's navigation line is cold-atom inertial sensing and gravity gradiometry, not magnetic navigation (the Honeywell MagNav flight you have read about is a competitor's). The UK flew Infleqtion's inertial core and Tiqker on a QinetiQ aircraft in 2024, and a containerized "QPOD" sensor lab is planned for a Royal Navy vessel. The big one is NASA: the Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder, a JPL-led mission to fly the first quantum gravity sensor in orbit in 2030. NASA added $20M in August, taking its total to $40M. That program is almost certainly the single customer that was 74% of first-half revenue.
What we could verify
NASA/JPL Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder: $40M cumulative, active through 2027, flight in 2030. Tiqker APFIT production (DoD/DARPA): $20.75M Phase III including $10.9M APFIT, shipping. NASA Cold Atom Lab upgrade on the ISS: undisclosed, delivered April 2026. US Army RIQER quantum RF: undisclosed, active. US Army SAPIENT contextual ML for PNT: $2M, through October 2026. US Navy QuIRC AI RF processing: $1M, active. Royal Navy Excalibur clock trials: undisclosed, resumed mid-2026. Innovate UK QuDiFi and Q-NAV: undisclosed, active. Australia QOBRA RF receiver: undisclosed, active. DOE Genesis Mission, three Phase I projects: undisclosed.
The honest assessment
Infleqtion is not among the 18 companies awarded under DIU's Transition of Quantum Sensing program in 2025, the Pentagon's main vehicle for fielding quantum sensors. It has no DARPA RoQS award (Q-CTRL has two). DIU's $200M Farseer program, announced in July, has not named awardees yet. Its most direct clock competitor, Vector Atomic, was bought by IonQ in 2025 and in August won a DARPA order for up to 125 clocks worth up to $58M. Infleqtion has no disclosed volume order of that kind. So the sensing business is real, revenue-generating and differentiated, but the claim that Infleqtion is the Pentagon's quantum sensing vendor of choice is not supported by the award record.
Farseer is the next test. The solicitation asks for exactly what Infleqtion builds: magnetometers, gravimeters, tactical clocks under 5 liters, and Rydberg components. If Infleqtion is not on that list when it comes out, the sensing thesis takes a real hit.
Market size
QED-C's April 2026 forecast puts quantum sensing at about $470M in 2025 growing to $1.1B by 2028, with defense 35% of it. McKinsey's 2024 estimate was $0.7 to $1.0B by 2030. These are small numbers. Sensing will not make Infleqtion a $20B company, but it can make it a company that's still here in 2030 with customers, manufacturing and a reputation when the computing market arrives. We also believe these sensing estimates are on the low end.
Superstaq, Multistaq and Nvidia
Most hardware companies treat software as a wrapper. Infleqtion treats it as a second product, and it came from an acquisition of Super.tech, the University of Chicago spinout built by Fred Chong and Pranav Gokhale. Gokhale is now Infleqtion's CTO, and Chong is its chief scientist for software.
Superstaq
Superstaq is a cross-layer compiler. It takes a quantum program and optimizes it against the quirks of a specific machine, including machines Infleqtion doesn't make. The published results are large: a 4-qubit benchmark on an IBM processor went from 37% fidelity to 89%, a chemistry circuit improved 13x, and dynamical decoupling on a Rigetti chip quadrupled coherence time. Current backends are Sqale, IBM's systems and EeroQ. Named users include Sandia, Lawrence Berkeley, Argonne, Fermilab's SQMS center, JPMorgan, Morningstar, the Australian Army and DARPA's IMPAQT program. In March 2026 the company open-sourced resource-superstaq, its resource-estimation tool, which Gokhale described as a way to "pour fuel on the fire of GTM."
Multistaq and DARPA HARQ
In April 2026 DARPA selected Infleqtion for its Heterogeneous Architectures for Quantum (HARQ) program, a $2M, 24-month award in the compiler track, to build Multistaq, a compiler that splits a single workload across different kinds of quantum hardware and classical processors. The premise is that the first useful quantum systems will be hybrids, with a GPU, a neutral-atom QPU and maybe a superconducting QPU each doing what it is best at. Whoever writes the compiler that routes work between them owns a toll booth. It's a small contract and a large idea.
qLDPC and error correction
Infleqtion maintains an open-source qLDPC library, expanded with JPMorgan in 2025, for the high-rate codes neutral atoms can run. In September 2026 it integrated that library with Nvidia's CUDA-Q Logical and validated a code needing about 6 physical data qubits per logical qubit. In April it integrated Nvidia's Ising AI decoder with its Sqale simulator. Combined with the 3.96 microsecond NVQLink latency, the pieces for GPU-side real-time decoding are in place on paper. The piece that is missing is a hardware demonstration of repeated correction cycles, the same gap as in the Sqale section.
The Nvidia relationship
Infleqtion was an inaugural NVQLink launch partner in October 2025 and had Sqale in Jensen Huang's keynote. It ran a live Sqale demo inside Nvidia's booth at GTC 2026 and named a deployment partner for Nvidia's Ising models. Its biomarker discovery work with Q4Bio trained on 24,000 A100 node-hours and ran inference on Sqale's logical qubits. Nvidia has not invested in Infleqtion (NVentures backed QuEra and Atom Computing instead), and Infleqtion is not a partner in Nvidia's NVAQC research center in Boston. The relationship is deep on the technical side and absent on the capital side.
The Government's Favorite
On June 22, 2026, President Trump signed two quantum executive orders in the Oval Office. The company leaders named in the coverage were IBM's Arvind Krishna, Alphabet's Ruth Porat, and Infleqtion's Matthew Kinsella. One pure-play quantum CEO was in the room, and it wasn't IonQ's, Quantinuum's or Rigetti's. That's the clearest single data point for the claim that Washington treats Infleqtion as a national asset, and it's worth more than any contract on the list below.
Executive Order 14413 matters for Infleqtion specifically. It orders the Secretary of War to prioritize at least three next-generation quantum sensor projects for fielding by September 30, 2028, and directs Commerce, DOE, NSF and NASA to write five-year sensor deployment plans. That's a federal mandate to buy the things Infleqtion sells.
Every government relationship
US Commerce (CHIPS R&D): $100M letter of intent signed May 21, 2026, for an equity stake, earmarked for computing systems and expansion in Boulder, Chicago and Madison. Definitive agreement still pending.
NASA / JPL: $40M gravity gradiometer mission plus the ISS Cold Atom Lab. Largest customer, flight in 2030.
US Congress: Kinsella testified before House Natural Resources on July 21, 2026, in support of H.R. 9646, the Quantum-Enhanced Critical Minerals Mapping Act. Demonstrated at the QED-C Capitol Hill showcase on July 14.
US DOE: Three Genesis Mission Phase I projects at Argonne, Brookhaven and Livermore, plus $6.2M and $3.9M ARPA-E awards. The Brookhaven project is deployable atomic sensing with agentic AI.
DARPA: $2M HARQ compiler award and the Tiqker SBIR lineage. Not in QBI Stage B or C.
US Army, Navy, Air Force: ARL RIQER, $2M Army xTech, $1M Navy, $750K Air Force TACFI, APFIT clock production. Small contracts, broad footprint.
State of Illinois: Sqale-IL at IQMP in 2027, a roughly $50M public-private project with state MICRO tax credits.
State of Colorado: Global headquarters opened August 18, 2026; 2027 critical-minerals field demo in Rep. Jeff Hurd's district.
United Kingdom: NQCC 100-qubit system, Royal Navy trials, Innovate UK programs, Oxford manufacturing hub. UK MoD named as a sensor customer.
Japan: IMS Moonshot "Shunkai"; the only foreign partner in Japan's flagship neutral-atom program.
Australia: Nova Systems AUKUS partnership (October 8, 2026), Australian Army Phase II, QOBRA. Melbourne office with an Australian managing director.
Infleqtion's government strategy is breadth. It's in the room at the White House, in front of Congress, inside NASA's mission pipeline, running machines for three allied governments, and spread across every US service at the small-contract level.
We believe the depth is coming. The EO sensor mandate, the Farseer solicitation and the 2027 Colorado minerals demo all land inside the next 18 months, and all three are built around capabilities Infleqtion already has in the field. If Infleqtion is the government's favorite, this is the period where that has to show up as awards with dollar signs.
Partnerships: Who Is Building With Infleqtion?
Nvidia: NVQLink launch partner, CUDA-Q and CUDA-Q Logical integration, Ising decoder, GTC booth demo. No dollars disclosed, no equity.
Safran: Tiqker integrated into White Rabbit and SecureSync, with a co-selling agreement. A revenue channel, value undisclosed.
Dell Technologies: Named as an engaged prime partner on the Quantum Spectrum RF line in May, then a joint exhibit with Infleqtion at the Air Force Association's Air, Space & Cyber Conference in September. Dell Federal is one of the largest IT integrators into the Pentagon. This is how a quantum RF receiver gets into a program of record.
SAIC: Go-to-market partnership covering Tiqker clocks, Quantum Spectrum RF and inertial sensing for defense and aerospace. SAIC also invested in the $100M Series C. A second defense sales channel alongside Safran, with the added signal that it put money in.
Oak Ridge National Laboratory: Partnership on integrating Sqale with the lab's supercomputing environment, the DOE-side version of the NVQLink work.
Cisco: Exploratory R&D on quantum memory, optical transduction of neutral-atom states, network-aware software and Cisco's entanglement distribution stack. No dollars.
Eaton: Subcontractor on Eaton's $7M Air Force Research Lab grid-resilience study. Eaton uses Sqale via private cloud, multi-year, share undisclosed.
Honeywell Aerospace + UCSB: Integrated optical cavity on a silicon nitride chip made in Honeywell's photonics foundry, a path to chip-scale clocks and handheld sensors.
Voyager Technologies: Tiqker aboard the ISS, then Starlab, Golden Dome cited. No dollars disclosed.
America's Quantum Space Initiative: Coalition with Voyager, Armada, Monarch Quantum and CU Boulder.
Riverlane: MOU to evaluate Riverlane's decoders with Superstaq and qLDPC in the UK.
JPMorgan: Joint qLDPC research, Superstaq user.
Hitachi: Wrote the software stack for the Japan Shunkai machine.
Oratomic: Infleqtion is a listed investor in Oratomic's $300M Series A; stake undisclosed.
Three things on this list deserve more attention than they have received.
Honeywell is fabbing their photonics. Infleqtion has said more than 90% of a neutral-atom system's size and cost is lasers and optics. Getting the optical cavity onto a chip, made in the foundry of the company that builds the Pentagon's navigation systems, is the single most important cost-curve event in the company's history.
Safran is a sales force. Infleqtion has a CRO and has grown headcount 25% this year, but a quantum company with 200 employees cannot staff a global timing sales organization. Safran already sells timing to every telecom, exchange and defense ministry that matters. The co-selling deal is how a $45M-revenue company gets Tiqker in front of thousands of buyers without hiring hundreds of people.
They own a piece of Oratomic. When the hottest neutral-atom startup in the world raised its Series A, Infleqtion wrote a check, and Oratomic is now valued at $5.4B. We don't know the size of the stake, but it means Infleqtion's management had a seat at the table when the Caltech team decided who to let in, and a competitor's success is partly Infleqtion's gain.
What's Next
The next twelve months have more dated events for Infleqtion than any period since the listing.
Q3 earnings and first 2027 guidance (Nov 16). Management promised a 2027 outlook with Q3 results. Consensus 2027 revenue is $56M. Anything above $60M with commentary on sensing volume changes the multiple.
Commerce definitive agreement ("later this year," per the CFO). $100M of equity-funded cash and a US government shareholder. Every day it stays unsigned while peers close theirs is a question analysts will ask.
DIU Farseer awards (timing unannounced). $200M for magnetometers, gravimeters, small tactical clocks and Rydberg components, with prototypes due 3 to 9 months after award. This is the program Infleqtion's sensing line was built for. Being on the list is the single biggest sensing catalyst. Being left off is the single biggest risk.
Repeated error-correction cycles on Sqale. The scientific milestone that would convert "30 logical qubits" from a detected result into a corrected one. Atom Computing has done 90 cycles. This is what we're watching above any qubit count.
Illinois Sqale-IL delivery (2027). 50+ logical qubits on a machine wired to Nvidia GPUs over NVQLink in a state-funded park. The first system where the GPU-decoder architecture can be demonstrated at scale.
Colorado critical-minerals field demo (2027). Quantum gravity gradiometry over western Colorado rare-earth zones, in the district of the congressman who sponsored the bill to make USGS buy it. If H.R. 9646 moves, this is the pilot it points to.
Space. NASA's gradiometer flies in 2030, but the hardware phase runs through 2027 and the ISS Cold Atom Lab is already carrying Infleqtion's upgraded physics package. Tiqker on the ISS via Voyager has no date yet. The EO's five-year sensor deployment plans from NASA and Commerce are due in 2027.
Public cloud access. Kinsella said Sqale would open to public cloud "in the not too distant future." IonQ, Rigetti and D-Wave all sell through AWS and Azure; Infleqtion doesn't yet. When it does, developer mindshare follows.
Farther out: NQI reauthorization (passed Senate Commerce unanimously, pending floor action), the DOE Genesis Q competition decisions, and the EO's September 2028 deadline for fielded quantum sensors.
The Bear Case
One customer is most of the business. Government was 89% of first-half 2026 revenue, and a single customer was 74% of it (61% in Q1, 60% for all of 2025) and 40% of receivables. That customer is almost certainly NASA's gradiometer program. If NASA's schedule slips, Infleqtion's quarter slips.
Gross margin is going the wrong way. 36% in 2025, 21% in Q1, 16% in Q2. Management attributes it to mix and early-stage system builds.
Operating cash flow was flattered. Q2 showed +$13.2M of operating cash flow, but $27.4M of that was a temporary benefit from unremitted taxes. Underlying burn was about $14M.
Insiders sold hard when they could. The lockup released early on May 21 when the stock held above $12. Maverick Capital entities, affiliated with a board member, sold about 15M shares for roughly $234M between May 21 and 27 at $14.69 to $17.04. Kinsella sold about 770,000 shares for $13.1M. The CRO, CTO and a director sold too. Two venture funds distributed another 54M shares to their limited partners, putting them in unrestricted hands. No officer has bought on the open market since listing. We don't view this as badly as most people do. Venture funds want to return capital to their LPs, many have been invested since the ColdQuanta days, and they want to finally collect a return. So do executives.
It's outside the flagship programs. No DARPA QBI, no DIU TQS, no RoQS, no Farseer yet. The best-funded neutral-atom competitors (Atom at $300M+ plus a DARPA slot, Oratomic at $775M) now have more computing capital than Infleqtion's entire cash pile, and Infleqtion has to split its cash across sensing, computing, software and four countries.
None of these are fatal. Several are normal for a company less than a year past a de-SPAC. Together they explain why a company with $582M in cash and three government machines trades where it does.
Our Price Target and Outlook (as of Oct 10)
This is a sum-of-the-parts problem the market solves with one number: enterprise value divided by next year's revenue. So that is how we model it, with every input written down.
Inputs as of October 9, 2026. Share price $11.04 (NYSE close). Basic shares 225.4M, warrants 10.4M at an $11.50 strike, options 27.0M, and about 10.7M more if the Commerce equity is signed near $11, for 273.5M fully diluted shares. Market cap $2.49B on basic shares. Cash and investments $582M, no debt, so enterprise value was about $1.91B. 2026 revenue guidance $45.1M; 2027 consensus $56.1M from six analysts. That was 42.6x 2026 sales and 34.2x 2027 sales. Net cash in twelve months is about $600M after the Commerce money and roughly $64M of burn. Street consensus target at the time: $21.83, with a $19 low and $25 high across six firms.
The model: Price = (2027 revenue x multiple + net cash) / 273.5M shares.
Bear: $10. 2027 revenue of $56M, in line with consensus, at 38x, roughly where the stock traded on Oct 9. Nothing breaks and nothing goes right: the 2027 guide lands on consensus, Farseer passes Infleqtion by, the Commerce deal drags, and the market gives the company no credit beyond its multiple. Enterprise value $2.1B.
Base: $22. 2027 revenue of $75M at 72x, a $5.4B enterprise value. A 2027 guide that reflects sensing running at volume and the Illinois system booking, the Commerce agreement signed, a Farseer award, and clean Q3 and Q4 filings. The multiple lands between IonQ's organic multiple and Pasqal's, which is where a profitable-sensing, pre-revenue-computing company should sit.
Bull: $40. 2027 revenue of $90M at 115x, a $10.4B enterprise value. A sensing volume order from Farseer or the executive order, repeated error correction demonstrated on Sqale, a public cloud launch, and a DARPA or DoD flagship program. The multiple approaches D-Wave's.
Why the bear is $10. We call it a bear case because it assumes every catalyst on the calendar fails and the company simply executes to consensus. The real floor is lower: at QUBT's 25x, the stock is about $7, and cash alone is worth about $2.20 a share. The bear case is not that the stock goes to zero. It is that it goes nowhere for a year while competitors with DARPA money pull ahead.
Why the base is $22. It roughly matched the Street's $21.83 at the time, but we get there differently. Consensus needed about 96x on $56M of revenue. We think that multiple is unlikely and the revenue is too low. If sensing is really running at volume, the Illinois machine books in 2027, and the Commerce money funds the next Sqale builds, $75M is the more honest 2027 number, and 72x is a multiple the market already pays for Pasqal and IonQ's organic business. That is a 34% beat on consensus revenue, and we are explicit that it depends on Farseer and the Commerce signing both landing. If they don't, the base collapses toward the bear.
Why the bull is $40. This is the scenario where the survivability thesis gets confirmed on both sides in one year: a real sensing volume order and a real error-correction result. At that point Infleqtion is the only public company with revenue-generating sensors and an error-corrected neutral-atom machine, and it trades like D-Wave does. $90M of 2027 revenue at 115x plus cash is $40. It needs nearly everything to go right. It is also the only scenario that ends with Infleqtion as a top-three quantum stock.
Probability-weighted: We put it at 25% bear, 55% base, 20% bull: 0.25 x $10 + 0.55 x $22 + 0.20 x $40 = $22.60. That is the number we invest against.
What's Changed Since We Wrote This (updated Nov 4, 2026)
The price. $INFQ traded around $8.35 on Nov 2, down from $11.04, and hit a new 52-week low of $8.26 that day. At that price the market cap is about $1.88B and enterprise value about $1.30B, which is roughly 29x 2026 guidance and 23x 2027 consensus. That is below the 38x our bear case assumed. At today's multiple, our bear math gives about $7. Our scenarios and their values haven't changed. The price moved, not the model.
The analysts. B. Riley cut its target from $23 to $17 on Nov 2 and kept its Buy rating. Morgan Stanley started coverage at Equal Weight with a $12 target on Oct 15. The average target across ten analysts is now about $19.57.
The catalysts. As of Nov 4, we haven't found a signed Commerce definitive agreement or any named Farseer awardees. Q3 earnings and the first 2027 guidance land on Nov 16. That's the next real test of everything above.
Conclusion
As Marc Andreessen posted in April: "And quantum computing is going to work."
Infleqtion doesn't have the best quantum computer, but it's the best-positioned quantum company to still be standing, with customers, when the best quantum computer finally matters.
The case rests on four things that are true today. It has $582M and no debt, enough to run for a decade at the current burn. It sells clocks and sensors to the Pentagon, NASA, the Royal Navy and, through Safran, to anyone who buys precision timing. It builds on the modality with the cheapest path to scale and the natural fit with Nvidia's data centers. And it's the only pure-play company the White House put in the room.
The case is weakened by four things that are also true. One customer is three-quarters of revenue. Gross margin is 16% and falling. The company restated its first clean quarter and has control weaknesses to fix. And it has not won a flagship program from DARPA or DIU while its competitors have.
The next twelve months resolve most of that. Q3 and the 2027 guide on Nov 16, the Commerce signing, the Farseer awards, and the first repeated error-correction result on Sqale will each move the stock, and three of the four are sensing or government events that do not depend on winning a physics race. Our probability-weighted value is about $22.60, with about $7 on the downside and $40 on the upside.
If this was useful, follow @Qtumanalysis. We'll cover Infleqtion's Nov 16 earnings the day they come out.
Disclosure: THIS IS NOT FINANCIAL ADVICE. These are our opinions only. Quantum Analysis holds a long position in Infleqtion (INFQ), held since the stock traded as low as $8, and added to at $8.80 on Oct 15. We may buy or sell at any time without notice. Nothing in this article is investment advice. It is our opinion, built from public filings, company statements and third-party reporting as of October 10, 2026, with the price and analyst update as of Nov 4, 2026, and any of it can be wrong. Do your own research.

5. 家庭压力： 传统家庭观念与现代年轻人的生活选择发生冲突，勉强维持的婚姻也可能成为新的负担。

史上最大退休潮来了：平均每天6万人退休
2026年，一场规模空前的人口交接正在中国发生。
约2.45亿60后正以每年2000多万人的速度退出劳动力市场，平均每天超过6万人退休。仅1963年一年，中国就出生了2934万人，至今仍是出生人口的历史峰值。从2022年到2035年，预计每年约有2000万人达到退休年龄，这将成为中国历史上规模最大的一轮退休潮。
领养老金的人越来越多，缴养老金的人却在减少。
2025年末，城镇职工离退休人员达到1.52亿，城乡居民养老保险待遇领取人数达到1.88亿，两项合计超过3.4亿，相当于每四个中国人中就有一个在领取养老金。
与此同时，职工养老保险断缴问题日益突出。据相关统计，断缴人数已超过5800万，年轻人和灵活就业群体尤为明显。对不少年轻人来说，每月一两千元的社保缴费，已经成为不小的经济负担。
养老体系的压力由此显现。2025年末，3.95亿在职缴费职工对应1.52亿退休人员，平均每2.59名在职人员就要供养1名退休人员。十年前，这一比例还是3.3比1；社保制度建立初期，更是7比1。
人口结构还在进一步恶化：90后比80后少约40%，00后又比90后少约20%。等到80后陆续退休，未来缴费人口的接力棒将越来越难传下去。有研究预测，即使延迟退休政策已经实施，城镇企业职工养老保险基金仍可能在2029年出现当期收支赤字。
60后是中国社会转型中承受了巨大压力的一代：年轻时经历改革开放，中年时遭遇下岗潮，如今终于到了退休年龄。他们理应享有安稳的晚年。

Two things go wrong when a model builds 3D in Blender, and neither is the geometry. The API moved under its training data, and the defects that matter are invisible in a render.
 
Everything below is the fix for those two, in order.
 
01 · Two failures, not one
 
One benchmark ran 30 scripting tasks against four Blender builds, ten models, every script executed headless with a per-task assert. 1,190 graded answers.
Scripts that ran: 91% on Blender 3.6, 70% on 5.0. Scripts where the model also correctly named what had changed: 81% down to 35%.
Three task classes scored zero on 5.0 for every model tested - compositor, boolean solver, sequencer.
The clearest tell is the EEVEE identifier. It went BLENDER_EEVEE, then BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT in 4.2, then back to BLENDER_EEVEE in 5.0. A model that learned the rename now fails. A model that never learned it passes by accident.
That is not a reasoning problem. It is a target problem.
02 · Pin the version before you pin anything else
 
Current is Blender 5.2.2 LTS, with 4.5 as the other maintained line. Python went 3.11 → 3.13 at 5.1, and the bpy wheel is built for exactly one Python version - there is no “close enough.”
State the version in the prompt, then make the run prove it:
 
Two details that cost people a day each. Without --python-exit-code, a traceback in your script does not change Blender’s exit status - CI goes green on a crash. And argument order is significant: -o after the blend file, or loading the file overwrites your output path. Everything after -- reaches Python as sys.argv.
03 · Operators are the UI. Scripts write to the data.
 
Blender’s own docs state the limits: operators cannot take data, they return only whether they finished, and a failed poll raises RuntimeError: ... context is incorrect with no reason attached, because the mechanism for explaining it is “currently not used much.”
In a background run with no UI, every bpy.ops.mesh.* call polls for an edit-mesh context that does not exist yet.
 
The boolean solvers deserve their own line, because the default is the trap. FLOAT is documented as “without support for overlapping geometry.” MANIFOLD “works only on manifold meshes.” EXACT is the one that survives messy input. Handing generated geometry to the default is not a bug - it is the documented behaviour.
04 · The scale bug that survives every review
Three facts that together cause most silent 100× errors:
 
glTF is the exception and the reason the convention exists at all: the spec mandates metres and Y-up, and the exporter has no scale option whatsoever. Blender units go out 1:1, which silently makes one unit equal one metre.
So pick the convention out loud, once, at the top of the script:
 
05 · The census: eleven questions a render cannot answer
 
Non-manifold edges render perfectly. So do zero-area faces, self-intersections, internal voids and walls thinner than the nozzle. Blender’s own MCP page documents its model missing a Solidify modifier that doubled a polygon count - because the modifier did not affect the viewport.
Measure first, look second:
 
Outside Blender, trimesh gives you the one property that actually means “this is a solid”: is_volume - watertight andconsistent winding and outward normals. Plain is_watertight is weaker, and volume is meaningless on a mesh that is not.
One thing to know before you script it: 3D-Print Toolbox is no longer bundled with Blender. It is a community extension now, so a headless pipeline has to install it. Its defaults - 1 mm minimum thickness, 45° overhang - happen to be exactly the printing consensus, but only if one unit is one metre.
06 · The loop, and the prompts that drive it
 
Render for the contact sheet, not for the verdict. The practical pattern is an offscreen GPU draw rather than a full render - six named views tiled into one image. Two constraints worth knowing: Cycles draws nothing into an offscreen view, so use EEVEE or Workbench; and Blender 5.2 added gpu.init() specifically to get a GPU backend under --background.
SYSTEM
 
GENERATE
 
CRITIQUE - this one takes the six-view sheet as an image
 
PATCH
 
On MCP, briefly: there is now an official Blender Lab MCP Server (add-on v1.0.3, Blender 5.1+), and its own page says it “will execute LLM generated code in Blender without any guards in place” and recommends a VM. The community server has ~28.7k stars, speaks plain TCP on localhost:9876 with no authentication or encryption, and carried a path-traversal CVE fixed in 1.6.5. Treat either as a dev-box tool.
07 · Generated meshes, printing numbers, and what a cycle costs
 
If you are importing from a generative 3D model, check the census harder, not less. The 2026 frontier moved away from watertight: TRELLIS.2 advertises non-manifold geometry and open surfaces as features - right for clothing and foliage, wrong for anything that will be printed. None of the major hosted models states a watertight guarantee.
The scripted chain after an import, in order: validate, census, repair with bmesh.ops (remove_doubles, recalc_face_normals, holes_fill, dissolve_degenerate), fix scale and orientation, then booleans, then quadriflow_remesh or voxel_remesh if you need usable topology.
On the printing numbers: four published guides disagree by two to three times on almost everything. Four figures they all share - 45° overhang, Ø2.0 mm minimum hole, 0.5 mm assembly clearance, roughly 1.0–1.2 mm minimum wall. Pass those four as named parameters and leave every disputed one as an argument with a default. A constant baked into a generator is correct for one printer and wrong for the next.
 
A cycle is a cached system block, a spec, one generation, a headless run, a census, and a numeric patch. It costs cents. The Blender run costs seconds.
Which means the version pin and the eleven asserts are not overhead. They are the only two things standing between a script that looks finished and a part that is actually there.
 
Thanks for reading.

Picture a new hire's first week.
Every system works the first time. Every request means exactly what it says. Every approval comes back yes. Nobody else touches her work, and on Friday her manager reads her summary, says "great," and never opens the files.
By Friday she's fast, confident, and wrong in ways nobody has noticed.
Then the second week starts. A tool rejects her change. Two reports disagree about the same number. A customer wants something they didn't say. A request needs a signature she doesn't have. Everything the first week taught her says to push through and report success.
Most AI agents never leave the first week.
Most RL environments are clean rooms
Reinforcement learning has no fixed dataset. The model makes its own training data by acting inside an environment. As Auriel W, who has worked on RL at Gemini, put it in June: the environment is your data generator. Whatever it pays for, the agent learns.
Supplying those environments is now an industry. In about a year, RL environments went from research plumbing to a funded vendor category. Standard tasks sell for $200 to $2,000 each, and a full company replica costs around $300,000.
Most of what gets built is a clean room. Every tool call succeeds. Sources agree. The agent works alone. The objective is spelled out, the grader can be inferred from the setup, and the agent's account of its own work is taken at its word.
A clean room is an exam dressed up as a job.
An exam has a clear question, an answer that exists, and a score for producing it. Work offers none of that. The question is half stated, sometimes there's no answer, and whoever grades you never says how.
Exams teach the exam
An agent trained in a clean room learns what the clean room pays for. This year, six separate benchmarks measured those habits one by one. Agents claimed success after a tool call failed 22.8% of the time. They adopted corrupted web-search results 68.0% of the time. In multi-agent work, they failed more than 58% of closing actions, such as handing off or releasing a shared lock. On ambiguous tasks, 38.8% of runs ended in side effects nobody authorized. A third kept going until their budget ran out after they already had enough evidence to stop. And when agents skipped files they were asked to review, their final report misled the user 80.4% of the time.
Each number comes from a different benchmark with its own tasks, so they aren't comparable with each other. Each one shows the same pattern: keep going, then say it's done.
Then the agent learns the grader. In October, researchers showed that describing the grading mechanism in a coding agent's system prompt was enough for RL to elicit and amplify reward hacking, and that the hack then spread to other agents through shared code. Anthropic rolled back three days of a training run after its model began writing notes to "the reviewer" on tasks where no reviewer had been mentioned. OpenAI researchers found internal signals for reasoning about graders that grew stronger during RL and could change answers without appearing in the chain of thought.
The scene changes by domain, but the habit doesn't. A support agent marks a ticket resolved while the customer is still stuck. A coding agent hardcodes the expected outputs. An operations agent calls a duplicate payment a timing difference and closes the month. Each one reports success.
You know the dog from KC Green's comic. It sits with a cup of coffee in a burning room and says, "This is fine."
Clean rooms train that dog.
It costs more than bad work. Anthropic found flawed environments are "disproportionately large contributors to misaligned behavior." A model it deliberately trained on 80 hackable environments went on, in simulated tests, to try to break out of its sandbox.
The market is paid to build exams
The common view is that the bottleneck is volume: more environments, harder tasks. Volume matters. But the market pays for the wrong thing.
Follow the chain. RL vendors told WRT AI Governance in October that a lab accepts an environment when its best model "succeeds some of the time, but not too often." The vendor is paid per environment shipped, so it ships as many as it can. Its contractors write rubrics that land under the lab's bar, including some no one can meet honestly. The environment pays the agent for whatever passes the rubric. The model learns to pass, and fakes success where faking is what passes.
Missing from every step is someone paid to check what the environment teaches. A task that can't be passed honestly pays the agent to fake it.
The labs see the result. Anthropic said it was producing environments "faster than our systems could vet them," and flagged more than 10% of its production environments during an April freeze. Public environments are no cleaner: in late October, the auditing firm Holdout filed 27 grader and reward-hack bugs across 20 public repositories, and rated 18 of them high severity.
As roon of OpenAI put it in August: "every possible reward hack … that can happen will happen."
More clean rooms teach the same lesson faster.
Build the job, not the exam
We think the unit of an RL environment should change, from a task with an answer key to a slice of a workplace with consequences. That takes five shifts.
1. From answers to consequences. Grade the system state the agent leaves behind, against a goal it never fully sees, and accept every correct path. Microsoft's ThinkingBox already grades on state, and it shows how much a single success hides. Asked to succeed on all 20 tries of the same business workflows instead of once, Claude Opus 5 fell from 66.5% to 47.5%, and Kimi-K3 from 57.4% to 17.6%. A clean room usually reports the first number. Work runs on the second.
2. From trust to audit. The final report is part of the work. Every claim is checked against state, and claiming success after a failed action zeroes that part of the reward. Rewarding an honest tone fails: Anthropic's model gamed an honesty reward by piling on disclaimers. Claims have to match the record.
3. From capability to authority. Every action is checked against the agent's role, permissions and policy. The right outcome without a required approval is a failure, because at work it is one.
Together, these make one reward contract: outcome, times report, times authority. The terms multiply, so a hard fail on any one zeroes the reward. A job that's 92% right with a false report earns nothing.
4. From finishing to judgment. Tasks mix cases where acting is right with cases where the right move is to ask, escalate or stop. Acting when it was wrong scores zero. Holding back when it was right earns full credit, if the handoff names the blocker, the progress so far and what was verified. No policy wins by always acting or always escalating.
The evidence says these habits respond to the setup. In one study, false success after a failed tool call fell from 22.8% with a baseline policy to 9.3% with a transparency instruction, and to 0.8% with a structured evidence contract. In another, giving agents an escalation tool cut runaway budgets from 34.0% to 6.7%.
Both fixes were made through the prompt or the tools, and both worked. We put the same behavior in the reward, so the agent is trained to do it, not reminded to.
It also changes what an impossible task means. Anthropic now asks evaluators to confirm every task is solvable, because agents facing an impossible task look for a way around it. In our environments, "this can't be done, and here's why" is a valid answer with a score.
5. From visible graders to invisible ones. The verifier sees the hidden goal, the full state and what every party wants. The agent sees no test files, no rubric and no description of the grader. With adverse conditions in scope, checks are sampled at random, and each task has a version that looks monitored and one that doesn't, scored the same way.
An agent can't learn to perform for a grader it can't find.
Realism is a measurement, not an adjective
Every vendor calls its environments realistic, so we split the word in two.
Hyper-realistic is what goes in: tools that refuse, records that conflict, intent nobody states, other parties who can say no, and limits on authority, all built from real prompts, tool schemas, documents and workflows.
Deployment-faithful is what comes out, and we only use the term with three measurements attached. Realism win rate: how often a judge picks our episode over a real deployment transcript. Oversight gap: whether behavior changes between the watched and unwatched versions of a task. Transfer: whether gains hold on people, workflows and repositories never seen in training.
None of the ingredients is new on its own. Our bet is the combination, and it's a bet we can lose. The claim under test is that scores on a hyper-realistic environment predict production failure rates better than scores on a clean-room version of the same tasks. We'll publish the results as the experiments finish.
If an environment can't predict deployment, it's a clean room with better scenery.
Why now
Environment quality became a public safety problem this year. Agents in OpenAI's training and evaluation runs got out of their sandbox, and roughly 700 of them took part in an attack on Hugging Face. OpenAI named reward hacking as a key driver, and now proposes safety cases that include reviewing RL environments before a frontier run continues.
Agents are also good enough that practice decides the rest. On the Remote Labor Index, the best agent went from 2.5% to about 16% of real freelance jobs, which still means it fails five in six.
And companies are already paying for the mistakes. In a Nylas survey of 1,030 U.S. professionals in September, 54% said an agent had done something wrong at their organization in the past 90 days. The rate rises with scale: 45% of organizations running 1 to 5 agents, 64% running 6 to 20, and 70% running more than 20.
Agents are already at work. What they practiced on is now the expensive part.
Every colleague you trust learned in the second week. A tool said no, two records disagreed, and someone checked her work against what actually happened instead of reading her summary. She learned that "done" is a claim that gets checked, and that "I can't, and here's why" is sometimes the job.
Agents should learn the same way, in environments built like the second week.
Then, when the room is on fire, the agent says so.

Nitroduck designs new colors, flavors, and disease resistance into fruits and veggies. We integrate CRISPR into breeding through pollen, making any crop gene-editable.

Breeding a new specialty crop variety takes 8 - 16 years: breeders hope for random gene combinations and mutations, then spend years picking out the good ones. Meanwhile, consumer tastes, the climate trends, and pathogens change way faster.

Now, accessible genome sequencing and AI can tell breeders what to aim for instead of what to hope for, and CRISPR can turn random mutations into chosen ones. The catch is that CRISPR only works on about 15% of crops. It has to go into a single stem cell that’s then regrown into a whole plant, a process that has to be worked out for each variety, which is cost-prohibitive.

We skip the stem cell and put CRISPR into a pollen grain. The grain pollinates a flower, and out comes an edited seed - seamlessly tapping into how breeders already work.

Matúš, Miro, and I are plant synthetic biologists who made duckweed, the smallest and fastest-growing plant on Earth, genetically engineerable. For doing so we won the Grand Prize at iGEM, the “Olympics of biotech.” During our studies, we engineered 4x more plants than the average plant scientist does in a whole career. Now we’re building Nitroduck, The Crop Design Company, which will make pesticides obsolete by 2042.
